title: The Index (Staging Area)
description: Understand the Git index, how it differs from the working directory and HEAD, and how to inspect it directly.

data.text: The Git index (also called the staging area or cache) is the middle layer between your working directory and the last commit. When you run git add, files are copied into the index. When you run git commit, the index becomes the new tree. Understanding the index is essential for staging partial changes and writing Git scripts.

Git's mental model has three trees: the working directory, the index (staging area), and HEAD. Each tracks a different state of your files. git add moves content from the working directory into the index. git commit moves content from the index into a new commit, updating HEAD.

data.title: The three states
items: **Working directory** — Actual files on disk. Edits go here first.
**Index (staging area)** — A snapshot of the next commit. Populated by git add.
**HEAD** — The last commit on the current branch. Updated by git commit.

data.title: Track file states across add and commit
data.code:
# Edit a file
vim src/Program.cs

# See what changed in the working directory (unstaged)
git diff

# Stage the change
git add src/Program.cs

# See the staged diff
git diff --cached

# Commit
git commit -m "refactor: simplify Program.cs"

# All three trees are now aligned

data.title: Stage changes selectively
data.text: Use git add -p to stage hunks interactively. This lets you commit related changes together while leaving unrelated edits unstaged for a later commit.
The index is a binary file at .git/index. Use git ls-files to see its contents, git status to see the difference between the three trees, and git diff --cached to see staged changes.

data.title: Inspect the index
data.code:
# List everything staged in the index
git ls-files --stage

# Show index entry for a specific file
git ls-files --stage src/Program.cs

# See what changed between index and HEAD
git diff --cached --stat

# Unstage a file (keeps working directory changes)
git restore --staged src/Program.cs

# Reset index to match HEAD (discard all staged changes)
git reset HEAD

data.text: During a merge conflict, the index holds multiple versions of the same file at different stages. Stage 1 is the common ancestor, stage 2 is HEAD, and stage 3 is the incoming branch. Use git ls-files --stage to see them.

data.title: Inspect conflict stages in the index
data.code:
# During a merge conflict, see all stages
git ls-files --stage src/Program.cs

# Output shows three lines:
# 100644 <sha1> 1 src/Program.cs   (base)
# 100644 <sha2> 2 src/Program.cs   (HEAD)
# 100644 <sha3> 3 src/Program.cs   (incoming)

# Extract the base version
git show :1:src/Program.cs

# Extract HEAD version
git show :2:src/Program.cs

# Extract incoming version
git show :3:src/Program.cs

data.title: Do not edit the index binary directly
data.text: The .git/index file is a binary format. Never edit it with a text editor. Always use git commands like git ls-files, git update-index, or git read-tree to manipulate it safely.

items.question: Why does Git have an index at all?
items.answer: The index lets you stage specific changes and build a logical commit incrementally. Without it, every commit would need to include all current changes, making clean history much harder.

items.question: Can I have multiple staged versions of a file?
items.answer: Not in normal usage, but during a merge conflict the index holds multiple stages (ancestor, ours, theirs). After resolving, the index holds a single clean version.

items.question: What is the difference between git add -A and git add .?
items.answer: git add -A stages all changes everywhere (including parent directories). git add . only stages changes in the current directory. Use git add -A from the repo root for consistent behavior.

items.question: Does git restore --staged modify the working directory?
items.answer: No. git restore --staged only unstages the file from the index, leaving the working directory version untouched.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: The index sits between the working directory and HEAD
git add copies content from the working directory to the index
git commit snapshots the index into a new commit
git diff shows unstaged changes; git diff --cached shows staged changes
During conflicts, the index holds multiple stages of the same file
